questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (LBCF) addresses the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures in **Chapter 1: "Of the Holy Scriptures."**

This chapter is foundational to the entire confession, establishing the Bible as the ultimate authority for the Christian faith and practice. Its teachings on Scripture are heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) but are framed within a Baptist theological context.

Here is a breakdown of the key teachings found in Chapter 1 of the 1689 Confession:

### 1. Divine Inspiration and Authorship
The Confession teaches that the Scriptures are not merely human writings but are the very Word of God.
*   **God as Author:** It states that the Holy Scriptures are the "word of God written."
*   **The Holy Spirit:** The text was written by men who were "moved by the Holy Spirit."
*   **Purpose:** They were written to preserve the truth of God and to guide the church in faith and obedience.

### 2. The Canon (Which Books Belong)
The Confession explicitly defines the boundaries of the Bible, distinguishing between canonical books and other religious writings.
*   **The 66 Books:** It lists the books of the Old and New Testaments as the complete canon.
*   **Rejection of the Apocrypha:** It explicitly states that the Apocryphal books (books found in the Septuagint and Catholic Bibles but not the Hebrew canon) are not part of Scripture. They may be read for "edification of life," but they possess no authority and cannot be used to establish any doctrine of the faith.

### 3. Authority and Infallibility
The Confession establishes the supremacy of Scripture over all other authorities.
*   **Infallible Truth:** The Bible is described as containing "infallible truth."
*   **Supreme Judge:** It is the "supreme judge" in all controversies of religion. No church council, tradition, or personal revelation can override or add to the Scripture.
*   **Binding Authority:** Because it is God's word, it is binding on the conscience of believers.

### 4. Clarity (Perspicuity)
The Confession teaches that the Bible is clear enough for salvation.
*   **Not All Things Are Equally Clear:** It acknowledges that not every part of Scripture is equally plain.
*   **Necessary Things Are Clear:** However, those things necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are "so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them."

### 5. Necessity and Sufficiency
The Confession argues that Scripture is essential for the Christian life.
*   **Necessity:** While God's general revelation (nature and conscience) shows His power and divinity, it is not sufficient for salvation. The written Word is necessary because of the corruption of human nature and the insufficiency of general revelation to save.
*   **Sufficiency:** The Scripture contains "all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith and life." Therefore, nothing is to be added to it, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men.

### 6. Interpretation
The Confession provides guidelines on how Scripture should be understood.
*   **Scripture Interprets Scripture:** The "infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself." When a passage is difficult, it should be understood in light of clearer passages elsewhere in the Bible.
*   **The Role of the Spirit:** While the Spirit is the ultimate teacher, the Confession emphasizes that the Spirit does not speak *new* revelation but helps believers understand the written Word.
*   **Reason and Language:** It acknowledges the importance of understanding the original languages (Hebrew and Greek) and using reason to interpret the text, provided that reason is subject to the Word.

### 7. Preservation and Translation
*   **Original Languages:** The original manuscripts were written in Hebrew (Old Testament) and Greek (New Testament).
*   **Translations:** The Confession affirms that translations into the "vulgar" (common) languages are acceptable and necessary so that "the word of God may dwell plentifully in all."
*   **Worship:** It mandates that Scripture should be read in the public worship of the church.

### Summary: *Sola Scriptura*
In essence, Chapter 1 of the 1689 Confession is a robust defense of **Sola Scriptura** (Scripture Alone). It teaches that the Bible is:
1.  **God-breathed** (Inspired).
2.  **Complete** (Sufficient and Closed Canon).
3.  **Clear** (Perspicuous regarding salvation).
4.  **Authoritative** (The final rule for faith and life).

This doctrine serves as the foundation for the rest of the Confession, ensuring that every subsequent doctrine (on God, Christ, Salvation, the Church, etc.) is derived from and tested against the written Word of God.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the Second London Confession) addresses the doctrine of God and the Trinity in **Chapter 2**, titled *"Of God and of the Holy Trinity."*

This chapter is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and represents classic Reformed, Trinitarian orthodoxy. It is divided into two primary sections: one describing the nature and attributes of God, and the other defining the Trinity.

Here is a breakdown of what the Confession teaches on these subjects:

### 1. The Nature and Attributes of God (Chapter 2, Section 1)
The Confession begins by establishing strict monotheism and then details the metaphysical and moral attributes of the Divine.

*   **Monotheism:** It affirms that there is **"but one only, living, and true God."**
*   **Infinite Perfection:** God is described as infinite in being and perfection.
*   **Spiritual Nature:** God is a **"most pure spirit,"** meaning He is invisible, has no body, no parts, and no passions (meaning He is not subject to human emotional fluctuations or physical limitations).
*   **Eternity and Immutability:** He is immutable (unchanging), immense (omnipresent), eternal, and incomprehensible.
*   **Sovereignty:** God is almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, and most absolute. He works all things according to the counsel of His own immutable and most righteous will.
*   **Purpose:** All of God's actions are done **"for his own glory."**
*   **Moral Attributes:** The Confession balances God's sovereignty with His character. He is described as:
    *   Most loving, gracious, and merciful.
    *   Long-suffering and abundant in goodness and truth.
    *   Forgiving of iniquity, transgression, and sin.
    *   The rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.
*   **Justice:** Simultaneously, God is just and terrible in His judgments. He hates all sin and **"will by no means clear the guilty."**

### 2. The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity (Chapter 2, Section 2)
The second section of the chapter explicitly defines the Trinitarian nature of the Godhead, guarding against both polytheism (three gods) and modalism (one God appearing in three modes).

*   **Unity of Essence:** It teaches that within the **"unity of the Godhead,"** there are three persons.
*   **The Three Persons:** These persons are identified specifically as the **Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.**
*   **Equality:** The Confession states that these three persons are of the **"same substance, power, and eternity."**
*   **Distinction:** While they share the same essence, they are distinct persons.
*   **Worship:** Because they share the same substance and glory, the Confession implies that all three persons are to be worshipped and glorified equally (though the specific instruction on worship is often elaborated in later chapters regarding religious worship).

### Key Theological Implications
*   **Rejection of Materialism:** By stating God is a spirit "without body, parts, or passions," the Confession rejects any view that God is physical or subject to human limitations.
*   **Rejection of Arianism:** By stating the Son and Spirit are of the "same substance" as the Father, it affirms the full deity of Christ and the Holy Spirit, rejecting the idea that they are created beings.
*   **Rejection of Unitarianism:** By affirming three distinct persons in one Godhead, it rejects the idea that God is a single person.
*   **Rejection of Polytheism:** By affirming "one only... God," it rejects the idea of three separate gods.

### Historical Context
It is important to note that Chapter 2 of the 1689 Confession is nearly identical to **Chapter 2 of the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)**. This demonstrates that the Particular Baptists who wrote the 1689 Confession held the same orthodox views on the nature of God and the Trinity as the Presbyterian and Congregationalist divines of the Westminster Assembly. The Baptist distinctives (such as believer's baptism and the autonomy of the local church) appear in later chapters, but the foundational theology regarding God remains in full agreement with historic, creedal Christianity.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (LBCF) addresses the doctrine of God's decree primarily in **Chapter 3**, titled "Of God's Decree." This chapter is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and reflects a classic Reformed (Calvinistic) theological perspective.

Here is a summary of what the 1689 Confession teaches regarding God's decree, broken down by its key theological points:

### 1. The Nature and Scope of the Decree
*   **Eternal and Unchangeable:** The Confession teaches that God, from all eternity, did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass (Chapter 3, Section 1).
*   **Purpose:** The ultimate end of this decree is the manifestation of His own glory.
*   **Comprehensive:** Nothing happens by chance or outside of God's sovereign plan. Everything that occurs is within the scope of His decree.

### 2. God and Sin
*   **Not the Author of Sin:** The Confession is very careful to distinguish between God's sovereignty and human responsibility. It states that while God ordains events, He is **not the author of sin**, nor does He violate the will of His creatures.
*   **Secondary Causes:** God's decree does not destroy the liberty or contingency of second causes (human choices, natural laws). Instead, it establishes them. Humans act freely, yet their actions still fulfill God's sovereign plan (Chapter 3, Section 2).

### 3. Election and Reprobation
This is the most distinct part of the doctrine of decree in the Confession. It teaches a "double decree" regarding angels and men:
*   **Election:** Some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life. This is not based on any foreseen faith, good works, or perseverance in them. It is solely based on God's sovereign good pleasure and grace (Chapter 3, Section 3).
*   **Reprobation:** Others are foreordained to everlasting death. This is described as God passing over them and leaving them in their sin to face the punishment they deserve. This serves to display the glory of His justice (Chapter 3, Section 3).
*   **Unconditional:** Both election and reprobation are unconditional. They do not depend on human merit or foreseen response.

### 4. The Certainty of the Elect
*   **Definite Number:** The Confession teaches that the number of the elect is so certain and definite that it cannot be either increased or diminished (Chapter 3, Section 4).
*   **Known to God:** While the specific number is known only to God, the doctrine assures believers that their salvation is secure because it rests on God's eternal purpose, not their own fluctuating will.

### 5. Pastoral Application
The Confession concludes the chapter by instructing how this doctrine should be handled practically:
*   **Prudence and Care:** The doctrine of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care.
*   **Humility and Assurance:** When treated correctly, it should lead to humility (recognizing salvation is all of grace), praise (glorifying God), and assurance (knowing one's salvation is secure).
*   **Warning:** It warns that treating this doctrine with presumption (thinking one is saved without evidence) or despair (thinking one cannot be saved) is a misuse of the doctrine (Chapter 3, Section 5).

### Related Chapters
While Chapter 3 defines the *decree*, other chapters explain how it is executed:
*   **Chapter 5 (Of Providence):** Explains how God governs all things according to His decree, sustaining and directing creation.
*   **Chapter 10 (Of Effectual Calling):** Explains how the decree of election is applied to individuals through the Holy Spirit, calling them to faith.

### Summary
In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that **God is absolutely sovereign over all history.** He has eternally decreed everything that happens for His glory. This includes the salvation of the elect (based solely on grace) and the condemnation of the reprobate (based on justice). However, God remains holy and is not the author of sin, and human beings remain morally responsible for their actions.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of divine providence primarily in **Chapter 5: "Of Providence."**

As a Reformed Baptist confession, it aligns closely with the Westminster Confession of Faith on this topic but is tailored to Baptist distinctives. The chapter teaches that God is sovereign over all creation, that nothing happens by chance, and that God ordains all things while remaining distinct from sin.

Here is a detailed breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about divine providence:

### 1. Universal Sovereignty and Governance
The Confession begins by defining providence as God's active involvement in creation. It states that God "upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least."
*   **No Chance:** It explicitly rejects the idea of fortune or chance. Nothing happens "fortuitously" or without God's specific design.
*   **Purpose:** All events are directed toward God's own glory and the good of His creation.

### 2. The Relationship Between Decree and Events
The Confession teaches that because God has decreed all things, events happen "immutably and infallibly." However, it makes a crucial distinction regarding human agency:
*   **Secondary Causes:** God does not usually act by suspending the laws of nature (miracles) but works through "secondary causes." This means human decisions, natural laws, and physical events are real causes, yet they are ultimately under God's control.
*   **Human Freedom:** God's decree does not violate the nature of the creatures. Angels and humans act according to their own wills, yet their actions are encompassed within God's sovereign plan.

### 3. The Problem of Sin (Permission vs. Authorship)
One of the most theologically dense sections of Chapter 5 deals with how God relates to sin. The Confession maintains a high view of God's sovereignty while protecting His holiness:
*   **God is not the Author of Sin:** The Confession states clearly that God is "neither the author of sin, nor hath he any fellowship with it."
*   **Permission and Direction:** God permits sin to occur, but He does not commit it. He "limits, orders, and governs" sin to serve His own holy purposes.
*   **The Fall:** Even the fall of Adam was foreseen and permitted by God, yet the sin itself is attributed solely to the creature, not the Creator.

### 4. Special Providence for the Elect
While God governs all creation generally, the Confession teaches a "special providence" regarding the Church and the elect:
*   **Preservation:** God watches over His people to preserve them from falling away completely.
*   **Affliction:** When the righteous suffer, it is not because God has abandoned them. Rather, God allows affliction to test their faith, humble them, and sanctify them.
*   **Deliverance:** God is able to deliver His people from temptation and trouble, though He may choose to allow trials for their spiritual growth.

### 5. Providence and the Wicked
The Confession also addresses how providence relates to the ungodly:
*   **Hardening:** God may withdraw His grace from the wicked, leaving them to their own lusts and the temptations of the world.
*   **Judgment:** God uses the sins of the wicked to judge them. Their own rebellion becomes the instrument of their punishment.

### 6. Providence and Prayer
A common objection to strict providence is that if God has already ordained everything, prayer is useless. The 1689 Confession refutes this:
*   **Means of Grace:** Prayer is a "means" ordained by God to accomplish His ends.
*   **Duty:** The certainty of God's decree does not remove the duty of humans to pray or to use other means (like medicine for health or effort for work).
*   **Effectiveness:** Prayer is effective because God has ordained both the end (the answer) and the means (the prayer).

### Summary of Key Distinctions
To summarize the 1689 teaching, divine providence is characterized by:
1.  **Omnipotence:** God has the power to control all things.
2.  **Omniscience:** God knows all things before they happen.
3.  **Holiness:** God is not tainted by the evil He permits.
4.  **Wisdom:** God orders evil to bring about good (e.g., the crucifixion of Christ).
5.  **Human Responsibility:** Humans are still morally accountable for their actions, even though those actions fall under God's sovereign decree.

### Why This Matters
For the 1689 Baptists, this doctrine was not merely abstract theology; it was pastoral. It was designed to give believers **comfort** (knowing God is in control of their suffering) and **humility** (knowing they cannot boast in their own success, as it is God's grace). It assures the believer that no circumstance is outside the reach of God's care or His ultimate plan for redemption.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (LBCF)** teaches a robust form of **Reformed Covenant Theology**. It is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and the Savoy Declaration (1658), but it modifies specific points to align with Baptist distinctives, particularly regarding baptism and the nature of the church.

The primary teaching on covenants is found in **Chapter 7: "Of God's Covenant."**

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about God's covenants:

### 1. The Covenant of Works
The Confession begins by establishing that God entered into a covenant with Adam before the Fall.
*   **The Parties:** God and Adam (acting as the federal head of all mankind).
*   **The Condition:** Perfect and personal obedience.
*   **The Promise:** Life (eternal life) upon fulfillment of the condition.
*   **The Penalty:** Death (spiritual and physical) upon violation.
*   **The Result:** Adam broke this covenant through sin, bringing guilt and corruption upon all his descendants. Consequently, no human can be justified by the Covenant of Works (7.1–2).

### 2. The Covenant of Grace
Because humanity could not fulfill the Covenant of Works, God established a second covenant to save the elect.
*   **The Mediator:** Jesus Christ is the sole mediator of this covenant. He fulfilled the demands of the Covenant of Works on behalf of his people and bore the penalty for their sin.
*   **The Condition:** Faith in Christ. The Confession teaches that Christ's righteousness is imputed to believers, and they are justified by faith alone.
*   **The Promise:** Eternal life and salvation.
*   **The Scope:** This covenant is made specifically with the **elect** (7.3).

### 3. The Unity of the Covenant of Grace
A central tenet of the 1689 Confession is that there is essentially **one Covenant of Grace** administered differently throughout redemptive history.
*   **Substance:** The substance of the covenant is the same in both the Old and New Testaments. It is always based on grace, mediated by Christ, and received by faith.
*   **Administration:** The *administration* of the covenant differs.
    *   **Old Testament:** Administered through promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, and the Passover. These were "types and shadows" pointing to Christ.
    *   **New Testament:** Administered through the preaching of the Word and the sacraments (Baptism and the Lord's Supper). These are "more full and clear" revelations of the same grace (7.5–6).
*   **Continuity:** The Confession rejects the idea that the New Covenant is a completely different covenant with different terms. Rather, it is the same covenant of grace revealed more clearly after the coming of Christ.

### 4. The Baptist Distinctive: The Members of the Covenant
This is the most significant difference between the 1689 LBCF and the Westminster Confession (Paedobaptist).
*   **Westminster View:** The Covenant of Grace is administered to believers *and their children* (the visible church). Therefore, infants of believers are members of the covenant and should be baptized.
*   **1689 Baptist View:** The Confession teaches that the Covenant of Grace is made with the **elect** and their **spiritual seed** (7.3).
    *   While the *signs* of the covenant changed (circumcision to baptism), the *members* of the covenant are those who have faith.
    *   Because the covenant is spiritual and made with the elect, the sign of the covenant (baptism) is reserved for those who make a credible profession of faith.
    *   This theological framework is the basis for **Credobaptism** (believer's baptism) rather than Paedobaptism (infant baptism). The Confession argues that the New Covenant is distinct in that it is not a national covenant (like Israel) but a spiritual gathering of believers.

### 5. The Moral Law and the Covenant
The Confession clarifies the role of the Ten Commandments within the Covenant of Grace.
*   **Not for Justification:** The moral law (Decalogue) does not justify anyone. No one can be saved by keeping the law.
*   **Rule of Life:** However, the moral law remains binding on all people. For believers, it serves as a "rule of life" to show them God's will and to guide their gratitude, not as a means to earn salvation (19.1–6).

### 6. The "Covenant of Redemption" (Pactum Salutis)
While the 1689 Confession does not have a specific chapter titled "The Covenant of Redemption" (the eternal agreement between the Father and the Son), the concept is woven throughout the text.
*   It affirms that Christ was appointed by the Father to be the Mediator before the foundation of the world.
*   It teaches that Christ voluntarily undertook the work of redemption to fulfill the covenant promises (8.1–2).

### Summary of Key Differences from Paedobaptist Confessions
| Feature | Westminster Confession (Presbyterian) | 1689 London Baptist Confession |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Covenant Members** | Believers and their children (Visible Church) | The Elect (Spiritual Seed) |
| **Sign of the Covenant** | Baptism (including infants) | Baptism (believers only) |
| **Old vs. New Covenant** | One Covenant, different administrations | One Covenant, different administrations |
| **Basis of Baptism** | Covenant membership (via parents) | Personal Profession of Faith |

### Conclusion
The 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that God relates to humanity through two primary covenants: **Works** (broken by Adam) and **Grace** (fulfilled by Christ). It emphasizes the **unity** of the Covenant of Grace across history while maintaining a **Baptist distinctiveness** regarding who constitutes the covenant community. By defining the covenant as spiritual and made with the elect, the Confession provides the theological foundation for the practice of baptizing only those who profess faith in Jesus Christ.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of Christ the Mediator primarily in **Chapter 8**, titled *"Of Christ the Mediator."*

This chapter is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) but reflects the specific theological convictions of the Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists of that era. It outlines the person, work, and ongoing ministry of Jesus Christ as the sole bridge between a holy God and sinful humanity.

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about Christ as Mediator, organized by key theological themes:

### 1. The Person of the Mediator (The Hypostatic Union)
The Confession begins by establishing the nature of Christ, arguing that for mediation to be effective, the Mediator must be both fully God and fully man.
*   **Divine and Human:** Section 1 states that the Lord Jesus, in the "unity of two whole, perfect, and distinct natures," is one person. He is "very God and very man."
*   **Why this matters:** As God, His sacrifice has infinite worth; as Man, He can represent humanity and suffer death on their behalf.
*   **Sinlessness:** Section 3 emphasizes that He was "holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners." He was tempted in all points like us, yet without sin. This qualification is necessary for Him to be a perfect sacrifice.

### 2. The Appointment and Office
*   **Divine Appointment:** Section 1 notes that Christ was "ordained of God" to be the Mediator. This points to the eternal counsel of the Trinity (often associated with the Covenant of Redemption).
*   **The Covenant of Grace:** Section 1 also links His mediation to the "Covenant of Grace," stating He is the "surety" of this covenant. He stands in the place of the elect to fulfill the conditions of the covenant on their behalf.

### 3. The Work of the Mediator (Humiliation and Obedience)
The Confession details the "humiliation" of Christ, which includes His incarnation, life, and death.
*   **Active Obedience:** Section 4 states that Christ "did perfectly fulfill the law" and "suffered and died." This refers to His **Active Obedience** (perfectly keeping God's law) and **Passive Obedience** (suffering the penalty for sin).
*   **Substitutionary Atonement:** Section 4 clarifies that He offered Himself up to death "to make reconciliation for the sins of his people." This teaches that His death was a substitutionary sacrifice, satisfying God's justice.
*   **Anointing:** Section 4 mentions He was anointed with the Holy Spirit without measure to execute this office as Prophet, Priest, and King.

### 4. The Exaltation of the Mediator
The Confession moves from Christ's suffering to His victory.
*   **Resurrection and Ascension:** Section 5 affirms that He rose from the dead on the third day and ascended into heaven.
*   **Session at the Right Hand:** He now sits at the right hand of God the Father. This signifies His authority and the acceptance of His sacrifice by the Father.

### 5. The Ongoing Ministry: Intercession
A crucial aspect of Christ's mediation is that it is not finished at the cross; it continues in heaven.
*   **Intercession:** Section 6 teaches that Christ "ever liveth to make intercession for them." He continually pleads His finished work on behalf of believers before the Father.
*   **Judgment:** Section 6 also notes He will return to judge the world, asserting His authority as the Mediator who will ultimately separate the saved from the lost.

### 6. The Exclusivity of the Mediator
Perhaps the most practical application of this doctrine is found in Section 8.
*   **No Other Mediator:** The Confession explicitly states that there is "no other Mediator between God and man."
*   **Rejection of Saints and Priests:** It specifically rejects the idea that prayers should be directed to saints, angels, or the Virgin Mary. It asserts that Christ is the "only Mediator" and that believers should pray only to God in His name. This was a significant point of contention against Roman Catholicism and High Church Anglicanism at the time.

### 7. Imputation of Righteousness
Section 7 connects the mediation to the believer's justification.
*   **Imputed Obedience:** The Confession teaches that the "obedience and satisfaction of Christ" are "imputed" to believers.
*   **Justification:** Because of this mediation, believers are "freely justified" not by their own works, but by the work of Christ credited to their account.

### Summary
In the 1689 London Baptist Confession, Christ the Mediator is:
1.  **The God-Man:** Fully divine and fully human, without sin.
2.  **The Surety:** He voluntarily took the place of the elect in the Covenant of Grace.
3.  **The Sacrifice:** He fulfilled the law and died to satisfy divine justice.
4.  **The Intercessor:** He currently pleads for believers in heaven.
5.  **The Only Mediator:** No other being shares this office; salvation is found in Him alone.

This chapter serves as the soteriological (salvation) heart of the Confession, explaining *how* sinners can be reconciled to a holy God: solely through the person and work of Jesus Christ.

It correctly identifies the Reformed Baptist theological distinctives and avoids heterodox statements.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath predestinated unto Life, he is pleased in his appointed, and accepted time, effectually to call by his word, and Spirit, out of that state of sin, and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and Salvation by Jesus Christ; inlightning their minds, spiritually, and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his Almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his Grace. This Effectual Call is of God's free, and special grace alone, not from any thing at all foreseen in man, nor from any power, or agency in the Creature, coworking with his special Grace, the Creature being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses, until being quickned & renewed by the holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the Grace offered and conveyed in it; and that by no less power, then that which raised up Christ from the dead. Elect Infants dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit; who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth: so also are all other elect persons, who are uncapable of being outwardly called by the Ministry of the Word. Others not elected, although they may be called by the Ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will, nor can truly come to Christ; and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men that receive not the Christian Religion be saved; be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the Law of that Religion they do profess.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of effectual calling in **Chapter 10**, titled *"Of Effectual Calling."*

This chapter is nearly identical to Chapter 10 of the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), reflecting the Confession's strong Reformed (Calvinist) theology. It teaches that salvation is initiated and accomplished by God's sovereign grace, not by human merit or decision.

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about effectual calling, organized by its key theological themes:

### 1. The Source and Scope of the Call (Sections 1 & 6)
*   **Based on Election:** Effectual calling is reserved exclusively for those whom God has "predestinated unto life." It is not a universal call to salvation, but a specific call to the elect.
*   **God's Initiative:** It is entirely God's work. It flows from His "free and special grace alone," not from anything foreseen in the person (such as foreseen faith, good works, or merit).
*   **Exclusivity:** The Confession states clearly that "none are effectually called, except those whom God hath predestinated."

### 2. The Means of the Call (Section 1)
*   **Word and Spirit:** God calls His elect "by His Word and Spirit." This implies that the external preaching of the Gospel (the Word) is the instrument used by the Holy Spirit to accomplish the internal work.
*   **Location:** This calling takes place "out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature."

### 3. The Nature of the Transformation (Section 1)
The Confession describes the internal change that occurs during effectual calling using specific theological terms:
*   **Enlightenment:** God "taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them a heart of flesh." He enlightens their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God.
*   **Renewal of the Will:** God "renewing their wills." This addresses the doctrine of Total Depravity; because the natural will is dead in sin, it must be renewed by God so that the person *can* choose Christ.
*   **Determination:** God "determining them by His almighty power to that which is good."
*   **Willing Response:** Crucially, the Confession teaches that this divine determination does not coerce the person. Instead, it makes them "most freely" willing to come to Christ. The will is liberated to choose God.

### 4. Effectual vs. External Calling (Section 3)
The Confession distinguishes between two types of calls:
*   **The External Call:** This is the general preaching of the Gospel. The non-elect may receive this call and may even experience "common operations of the Spirit" (conviction, temporary joy, moral improvement).
*   **The Internal (Effectual) Call:** Only the elect receive this. Those who are not elect "never truly come to Christ," and therefore cannot be saved, regardless of how much they hear the Gospel.

### 5. Those Incapable of Hearing the Word (Section 4)
The Confession addresses a pastoral question regarding those who cannot hear the external call (such as infants or those with severe cognitive disabilities):
*   **Elect Infants:** It teaches that "elect infants, dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit."
*   **Sovereignty:** It acknowledges that while the ordinary means is the preaching of the Word, God is not bound by His own means. He can save those incapable of hearing the Word if they are among the elect.
*   **Caution:** However, it warns against speculating on who is elect, stating that those who are not outwardly called "are not to be judged" as saved or lost based on their inability to hear.

### 6. Timing (Section 5)
*   **Due Time:** The elect may be called at different times. Some are called in childhood, others in adulthood.
*   **Regeneration:** Even if they are not yet outwardly called, they are "regenerated by the Spirit in due time." This suggests that the internal work of the Spirit may precede the external profession of faith.

### Summary of the Theology
In summary, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that **effectual calling is a monergistic act of God.**
1.  **Monergistic:** God does the work; the human is passive in the initial act of regeneration (like Lazarus in the tomb being raised).
2.  **Irresistible:** Because the will is renewed by the Spirit, the elect *will* inevitably respond to the call.
3.  **Transformative:** It changes the nature of the person from spiritually dead to spiritually alive.
4.  **Soteriological:** It is the bridge between God's eternal decree of election and the actual experience of salvation in time.

This teaching stands in contrast to Arminian or Semi-Pelagian views, which suggest that the human will cooperates with God's grace in the initial act of salvation or that God's call can be resisted by the elect. The 1689 Confession asserts that the call itself creates the faith that receives it.

The only minor point is that the 'Enlightenment' section conflates two distinct phrases from the Confession ('enlightening their minds' and 'taking away their heart of stone').

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God Effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth, not by infusing Righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting, and accepting their Persons as Righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone, not by imputing faith it self, the act of beleiving, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their Righteousness; but by imputing Christs active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousnnss, they receiving, and resting on him, and his Righteousness, by Faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ, and his Righteousness, is the alone instrument of Justification: yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving Graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ by his obedience, and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are justified; and did by the sacrifice of himself, in the blood of his cross, undergoing in their stead, the penalty due unto them: make a proper, real and full satisfaction to Gods justice in their behalf: yet in asmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his Obedience and Satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for any thing in them; their Justification is only of Free Grace, that both the exact justice and rich Grace of God, might be glorified in the Justification of sinners. God did from all eternity decreeto justifie all the Elect, and Christ did in the fulness of time die for their sins, and rise again for their Justification; Nevertheless they are not justified personally, untill the Holy Spirit, doth in due time actually apply Christ unto them. God doth continue to Forgive the sins of those that are justified, and although they can never fall from the state of justication; yet they may by their sins fall under Gods Fatherly displeasure; and in that condition, they have not usually the light of his Countenance restored unto them, untill they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith, and repentance. The Justification of Believers under the Old Testament was in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of Believers under the New Tement.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** teaches a classic Reformed doctrine of justification, found primarily in **Chapter 11**. It aligns closely with the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) but includes specific clarifications relevant to the Baptist context, particularly regarding the relationship between the law and grace.

Here is a summary of the key teachings on justification according to the 1689 Confession:

### 1. The Basis: The Righteousness of Christ
The Confession teaches that justification is not based on anything inherent in the believer. Instead, it is based entirely on the work of Jesus Christ.
*   **Imputed Righteousness:** God justifies sinners by imputing (crediting) the "obedience and satisfaction of Christ" to them.
*   **Active and Passive Obedience:** This includes Christ's perfect life (active obedience) and His sacrificial death (passive obedience).
*   **Text:** *"Those whom God effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth... not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone."* (11.1)

### 2. The Means: Faith Alone
Justification is received through faith, but faith is not the *cause* of justification; it is the *instrument*.
*   **Instrumental, Not Meritorious:** Faith does not justify because it is a "work" or a virtue that earns God's favor. Rather, it is the empty hand that receives the gift of Christ's righteousness.
*   **Exclusion of Works:** No works of the law (moral, ceremonial, or civil) can contribute to justification.
*   **Text:** *"Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification: yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love."* (11.2)

### 3. The Source: Free Grace
Justification is an act of God's free grace. It is not a transaction where God is obligated to justify anyone based on their merit.
*   **Unconditional:** It is granted to those whom God has effectually called, regardless of their prior moral state.
*   **Text:** *"God doth justify the believing sinner... not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them."* (11.1)

### 4. The Permanence: Once Justified, Always Justified
The Confession teaches the security of the believer regarding their legal standing before God.
*   **Irrevocable:** Justification cannot be lost. While a believer may sin and lose the *sense* of God's favor or the assurance of salvation, their actual status as justified remains secure.
*   **Text:** *"They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace... they shall certainly be preserved."* (17.1 - *Note: While Chapter 17 covers Perseverance, Chapter 11.4 explicitly states justification cannot be lost.*)
*   **Specific Clause on Justification:** *"They are never totally nor finally fall from the state of justification."* (11.4)

### 5. Continuity: Old and New Testament Saints
The Confession affirms that the method of salvation has not changed throughout history.
*   **Same Gospel:** Old Testament saints were justified in the same way as New Testament saints: by faith in the promised Messiah (Christ), even though they looked forward to His coming rather than looking back at His finished work.
*   **Text:** *"Christ, in the work of mediation, acteth according to both natures... The same is true of the saints of the Old Testament."* (11.3)

### 6. The Relationship to the Law (Section 6)
Chapter 11, Section 6 is a distinct addition in the 1689 Confession (not found in the Westminster Confession) that addresses **Antinomianism** (the belief that grace frees believers from obeying moral law).
*   **Works as Fruit, Not Root:** While good works do not justify, true faith inevitably produces good works.
*   **Law as Rule of Life:** Believers are not under the law as a "covenant of works" (to earn salvation), but they are under the law as a "rule of life" (to guide their obedience).
*   **Text:** *"Although good works... cannot merit the pardon of sin... yet they are of the nature of the law of God... and are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith."* (11.6)

### Summary of Distinctives
Compared to other Christian traditions, the 1689 Confession emphasizes:
1.  **Legal Declaration:** Justification is a forensic (legal) act of God declaring the sinner righteous, not a process of making them internally righteous (which is Sanctification).
2.  **Sola Fide (Faith Alone):** Explicitly rejects the idea that faith is a "work" that contributes to merit.
3.  **Sola Gratia (Grace Alone):** Emphasizes that the sinner contributes nothing to their justification.
4.  **Baptist Distinctive:** Section 6 clarifies that while Baptists reject the law as a means of salvation, they do not reject the law as a guide for holy living, guarding against the error of "cheap grace."

In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that a sinner is declared righteous before God solely on the basis of Christ's righteousness, received through faith alone, by God's grace alone, resulting in a permanent standing that inevitably produces a life of obedience.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath accepted in the beloved, effectually called and Sanctified by his Spirit, and given the precious faith of his Elect unto, can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end and be eternally saved, seeing the gifts and callings of God are without Repentance, (whence he still begets and nourisheth in them Faith, Repentance, Love, Joy, Hope, and all the graces of the Spirit unto immortality) and though many storms and floods arise and beat against them, yet they shall never be able to take them off that foundation and rock which by faith they are fastned upon: notwithstanding through unbelief and the temptations of Satan the sensible sight of the light and love of God, may for a time be clouded, and obscured from them, yet he is still the same and they shall be sure to be kept by the power of God unto Salvation, where they shall enjoy their purchased possession, they being engraven upon the palm of his hands, and their names having been written in the book of life from all Eternity. This perseverance of the Saints depends not upon their own free will; but upon the immutability of the decree of Election flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ and Union with him, the oath of God, the abiding of his Spirit & the seed of God within them, and the nature of the Covenant of Grace from all which ariseth also the certainty and infallibility thereof. And though they may through the temptation of Satan and of the world, the prevalency of corruption remaining in them, and the neglect of means of their preservation fall into grievous sins, and for a time continue therein; whereby they incur Gods displeasure, and grieve his holy Spirit, come to have their graces and comforts impaired have their hearts hardened, and their Consciences wounded, hurt, and scandalize others, and bring temporal judgements upon themselves: yet they shall renew their repentance and be preserved through faith in Christ Jesus to the end.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** teaches the doctrine of the Perseverance of the Saints in **Chapter 17**, titled *"Of the Perseverance of the Saints."*

This confession is a Reformed (Calvinistic) document, and its teaching on this subject is nearly identical to Chapter 17 of the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646). The doctrine asserts that those who are truly regenerated and justified by God will continue in faith and holiness until the end and cannot lose their salvation.

Here is a breakdown of the specific teachings found in Chapter 17:

### 1. The Certainty of Perseverance (Section 1)
The confession teaches that true believers **cannot totally or finally fall away** from the state of grace. This security is not based on the believer's own will or strength, but on the unchangeable nature of God's decree and work.

*   **Divine Origin:** Perseverance is grounded in God's eternal decree of election, the efficacy of Christ's merit and intercession, the abiding of the Holy Spirit, and the "seed of God" (the new nature) within the believer.
*   **The Guarantee:** Because these divine factors are immutable, the believer is guaranteed to remain in a state of grace. The confession states: *"They whom God hath accepted... can neither totally, nor finally, fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved."*

### 2. The Reality of Sin and Discipline (Section 2)
While the confession teaches that a believer cannot *finally* fall away, it explicitly acknowledges that believers **can and do fall into sin**. This distinguishes the doctrine from a "license to sin" or a belief that Christians are immune to moral failure.

*   **Temptation and Corruption:** Believers may be overcome by temptations and the corruption of their flesh.
*   **Consequences:** When they sin, they incur God's displeasure, grieve the Holy Spirit, lose the sense of God's favor, and may experience a hardening of the heart or a wounding of their conscience.
*   **Preservation:** However, even in these states of spiritual decline, they are preserved by God. They are not cast off; rather, they are renewed to repentance. The confession notes that they are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.

### 3. The Means of Preservation (Section 3)
The confession outlines how this perseverance is maintained. It is not automatic or mechanical; it involves the ongoing work of God in the life of the believer.

*   **God's Power:** They are kept by the power of God.
*   **Through Faith:** They are preserved *through faith*. This implies that the evidence of salvation is continuing faith. If someone claims to be a believer but abandons the faith entirely and permanently, the confession implies they were never truly regenerated to begin with (a concept often summarized as "once truly saved, always truly saved," but with the caveat that true salvation produces enduring faith).
*   **Eternal Security:** The ultimate result is that they shall be eternally saved.

### Summary of Key Distinctions
To understand the 1689 Confession's view, it is helpful to distinguish between two concepts often confused:

1.  **Falling into Sin:** The confession affirms that true Christians *can* commit serious sins and experience spiritual backsliding.
2.  **Falling from Grace (Apostasy):** The confession denies that a true Christian can *totally and finally* abandon the faith and reject Christ permanently. If a person does that, the confession teaches they were never truly a part of the elect or regenerated.

### Biblical Basis Cited
The confession grounds these points in Scripture, referencing verses such as:
*   **John 10:28-29:** No one can snatch the sheep out of the Father's hand.
*   **1 Peter 1:5:** Believers are guarded by God's power.
*   **Philippians 1:6:** He who began a good work will bring it to completion.
*   **1 John 2:19:** Those who leave the community show they were not truly of it.

In summary, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that **salvation is eternally secure because God preserves the believer.** While believers struggle with sin and may experience periods of spiritual darkness, the power of God ensures that they will ultimately persevere in faith and receive eternal life.

It clearly distinguishes between falling into sin and falling from grace, and correctly identifies the divine basis for perseverance.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the last judgment?
questions.reference_answer: God hath appointed a Day wherein he will judge the world in Righteousness, by Jesus Christ; to whom all power and judgement is given of the Father; in which Day not only the Apostate Angels shall be judged; but likewise all persons that have lived upon the Earth, shall appear before the Tribunal of Christ; to give an account of their Thoughts, Words, and Deeds, and to receive according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil. The end of Gods appointing this Day, is for the manifestation of the glory of his Mercy, in the Eternal Salvation of the Elect; and of his Justice in the Eternal damnation of the Reprobate, who are wicked and disobedient; for then shall the Righteous go into Everlasting Life, and receive that fulness of Joy, and Glory, with everlasting reward, in the presence of the Lord: but the wicked who know not God, and obey not the Gospel of Jesus Christ, shall be cast into Eternal torments, and punished with everlasting destruction, from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. As Christ would have us to be certainly perswaded that there shall be a Day of judgement, both to deter all men from sin, and for the greater consolation of the godly, in their adversity; so will he have that day unknown to Men, that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful, because they know not at what hour, the Lord will come; and may ever be prepared to say, Come Lord Jesus, Come quickly, Amen.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of the Last Judgment primarily in **Chapter 33**, titled *"Of the Last Judgment."* It also relies on **Chapter 32**, *"Of the State of Man after Death and of the Resurrection of the Dead,"* to establish the context of the bodily resurrection that precedes the judgment.

Here is a summary of what the Confession teaches regarding the Last Judgment, based on the five sections of Chapter 33:

### 1. The Appointment and the Judge
The Confession teaches that God has appointed a specific day for the judgment of the world. This day is not known to men but is fixed by God's decree.
*   **The Judge:** Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is the appointed Judge. He will judge in perfect righteousness.
*   **The Scope:** The judgment is universal. It will include all people (both the living and the dead) and fallen angels.

### 2. The Purpose of the Judgment
The ultimate goal of the Last Judgment is the manifestation of God's glory.
*   **Mercy:** It will display the glory of God's mercy toward the elect (believers).
*   **Justice:** It will display the glory of God's justice toward the wicked (reprobate).
*   **Public Vindication:** It serves to publicly vindicate God's character and the reality of His governance over creation.

### 3. The Basis of Judgment
The Confession states that Christ will judge the world **"according to their works."**
*   **Comprehensive Knowledge:** The judgment will not be superficial. Christ will judge not only outward actions but also "the secrets of all hearts."
*   **Motives:** The motives and intentions behind actions will be exposed.
*   **Distinction:** While the Confession teaches elsewhere that believers are justified by faith alone (Chapter 11), Chapter 33 emphasizes that works serve as the evidence by which the final state of a person is publicly demonstrated and rewarded or punished.

### 4. The Eternal Destinies
The Confession outlines two distinct, eternal outcomes for humanity:
*   **The Wicked:** Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel will be cast into **"everlasting punishment."** This involves separation from the presence of God and conscious torment.
*   **The Righteous:** Those who have believed in Christ will enter into **"life eternal."** This involves receiving the fullness of joy and glory in the presence of God.

### 5. The Practical Purpose for Believers
The Confession concludes by explaining why this doctrine is revealed to the church. It is not merely for speculation but for practical application:
*   **Encouragement:** It is meant to comfort the afflicted and persecuted believers.
*   **Warning:** It serves as a warning to the wicked to repent.
*   **Holiness:** It is intended to encourage believers to pursue holiness and godliness, knowing they will one day give an account of themselves to God.

### Context: The Resurrection (Chapter 32)
To fully understand the 1689 view of the Last Judgment, one must look at Chapter 32. The Confession teaches that the Last Judgment is preceded by the **Resurrection of the Dead**.
*   All the dead will be raised with their physical bodies (though changed and glorified for the righteous).
*   The soul and body will be reunited.
*   This ensures that the judgment is not merely spiritual but involves the whole person (body and soul) receiving their due reward or punishment.

### Summary
In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches a **literal, future, universal, and final judgment** presided over by **Jesus Christ**. It emphasizes that this event will publicly vindicate God's justice and mercy, result in the eternal separation of the righteous and the wicked, and serve as a motivation for Christian holiness.

questions.response:
The question of whether "fallen man" (humanity after the Fall of Adam) can choose God of his own free will is one of the most debated topics in Christian theology. There is no single, universally agreed-upon answer; rather, the response depends entirely on which theological tradition one follows.

Here is a breakdown of the major perspectives on this issue.

### 1. The Reformed / Calvinist View (Monergism)
**Answer: No.**

*   **The Doctrine:** This view is based on the doctrine of **Total Depravity**. It teaches that the Fall affected every part of a human being, including the will. Consequently, the natural man is spiritually "dead" (Ephesians 2:1) and enslaved to sin.
*   **The Will:** While humans make choices daily, their will is in bondage to their sinful nature. They are free to choose what they desire, but because their desires are corrupted by sin, they cannot desire God. As Martin Luther wrote in *The Bondage of the Will*, the will is like a beast of burden; if God rides it, it goes where God wills; if Satan rides it, it goes where Satan wills.
*   **The Solution:** Because man cannot choose God, God must first regenerate the heart (give new spiritual life). This is called **Irresistible Grace**. Once God changes the heart, the person freely chooses God, but they could not have done so without that prior divine intervention.
*   **Key Verse:** *"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."* (John 6:44)

### 2. The Arminian / Wesleyan View (Synergism via Prevenient Grace)
**Answer: Yes, but only because God enables it.**

*   **The Doctrine:** This view agrees that the Fall damaged human nature and that man cannot save himself. However, it rejects the idea that the will is totally bound.
*   **The Will:** Arminians believe in **Prevenient Grace**. This is a grace that "comes before" salvation. It is given to *all* people universally to counteract the effects of the Fall just enough to restore the moral ability to choose God.
*   **The Solution:** God initiates the relationship by offering this enabling grace, but the individual must cooperate with it. The will is restored to a state of neutrality where it can accept or reject the Gospel.
*   **Key Verse:** *"The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!' And let the one who hears say, 'Come!' Let the one who is thirsty come; and let the one who wishes take the free gift of the water of life."* (Revelation 22:17)

### 3. The Roman Catholic & Eastern Orthodox View (Synergism)
**Answer: Yes, through cooperation with Grace.**

*   **The Doctrine:** Both traditions emphasize **Synergism** (working together). They teach that while grace is absolutely necessary for salvation, the human will must cooperate with that grace.
*   **The Will:**
    *   **Catholicism:** The Council of Trent taught that while humans cannot justify themselves without grace, the will is not so bound that it cannot assent to God's call. Humans have the freedom to accept or reject sanctifying grace.
    *   **Orthodoxy:** Emphasizes the healing of the image of God. While the Fall wounded human nature, it did not destroy the *image* of God within man. Humans retain the capacity to respond to God's energies, though they cannot achieve salvation without God's grace.
*   **The Solution:** Salvation is a partnership. God offers the grace, and the human will must say "yes" to it.

### 4. The Pelagian View (Historical Heresy)
**Answer: Yes, naturally.**

*   **The Doctrine:** Historically, Pelagius taught that the Fall did not damage human nature and that humans have the natural ability to choose good or evil without the necessity of divine grace.
*   **Status:** This view was condemned as heresy by the early Church (Council of Carthage, 418 AD) because it undermined the necessity of Christ's atonement. Most Christian traditions today reject the idea that man can choose God *without* any divine assistance.

### The Scriptural Tension
The reason this debate persists is that the Bible contains verses that seem to support both sides:

*   **Verses suggesting inability:**
    *   *"None is righteous, no, not one... no one seeks for God."* (Romans 3:10–11)
    *   *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot."* (Romans 8:7)
*   **Verses suggesting ability/responsibility:**
    *   *"Whoever comes to me I will never cast out."* (John 6:37)
    *   *"God... desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."* (1 Timothy 2:4)

### Summary
*   **If you ask a Calvinist:** Fallen man is spiritually dead and cannot choose God until God makes him alive.
*   **If you ask an Arminian:** Fallen man is sick, but God's grace restores the ability to choose, which man must then exercise.
*   **If you ask a Catholic/Orthodox:** Fallen man is wounded, but through grace, the will is healed enough to cooperate with God.

Despite these differences, almost all Christian traditions agree on the practical outcome: **The Gospel must be preached to everyone.** Regardless of whether the will is bound or enabled, the command is for humans to repent and believe, and the promise is that God will save those who do.

questions.response:
The question of whether an unregenerate person (someone who has not been "born again" or spiritually renewed by the Holy Spirit) can do anything spiritually good in God's sight is one of the most debated topics in Christian theology.

The answer depends heavily on how one defines **"spiritually good"** and which theological tradition is being consulted. Generally, the consensus across orthodox Christianity is that **faith is necessary for an act to be pleasing to God**, but traditions differ on the *capacity* of the unregenerate will to exercise that faith or perform good works.

Here is a breakdown of the major theological perspectives on this issue.

### 1. The Reformed (Calvinist) Perspective: Total Depravity
In Reformed theology, the doctrine of **Total Depravity** teaches that sin affects every part of a person's being, including their will and intellect.
*   **The View:** An unregenerate person is spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1). Therefore, they are incapable of doing anything that is truly "spiritually good" or pleasing to God.
*   **Civil vs. Spiritual Good:** Reformed theologians distinguish between "civil righteousness" and "spiritual righteousness." An unregenerate person can perform acts that are socially beneficial (feeding the poor, obeying laws, being honest). However, because these acts are not done in faith and for the glory of God, they are not spiritually meritorious.
*   **Key Scripture:**
    *   *Romans 8:7–8:* "The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so. Those who are in the realm of the flesh cannot please God."
    *   *Hebrews 11:6:* "Without faith it is impossible to please God."
    *   *Isaiah 64:6:* "All our righteous acts are like filthy rags."
*   **Conclusion:** No. Without regeneration, the motive and the nature of the act are tainted by sin, making it spiritually unacceptable to God.

### 2. The Arminian / Wesleyan Perspective: Prevenient Grace
Arminian theology agrees that humans are fallen and cannot save themselves, but it emphasizes **Prevenient Grace**.
*   **The View:** God extends a grace to all people that restores a measure of free will. This grace enables an unregenerate person to respond to the Gospel and choose to do good.
*   **The Nuance:** While an unregenerate person *can* do good, they cannot do so by their own natural power; they can only do so because God's grace is actively working on them. Once they exercise faith, they are regenerated.
*   **Conclusion:** Yes, but only because God enables them to. The "goodness" of the act is derived from the grace that preceded it, not from the unregenerate nature itself.

### 3. The Roman Catholic Perspective: Natural vs. Supernatural Good
Catholic theology makes a distinction between natural virtue and supernatural merit.
*   **The View:** An unregenerate person (one without sanctifying grace) can perform "natural good" acts (moral virtues like courage, temperance, or charity). These are good in a human sense and contribute to the common good.
*   **The Limitation:** However, for an act to be "spiritually good" in the sense of meriting salvation or increasing grace (*meritum de condigno*), the person must be in a state of grace (regenerated/baptized). Without sanctifying grace, acts cannot merit eternal life.
*   **Conclusion:** They can do natural good, but not supernatural good that pleases God for the purpose of salvation.

### 4. The Lutheran Perspective: Bondage of the Will
Martin Luther held a view similar to the Reformed tradition regarding the will.
*   **The View:** In his work *The Bondage of the Will*, Luther argued that the unregenerate will is in bondage to sin. It cannot turn toward God.
*   **Coram Deo vs. Coram Homine:** Luther distinguished between standing before God (*coram Deo*) and standing before men (*coram homine*). An unregenerate person can be a good citizen, a good parent, or a good neighbor in the eyes of society. However, before God, their works are sinful because they are not done in faith.
*   **Conclusion:** No spiritually good works before God; only civil good works before men.

### Summary of the Core Disagreement
The crux of the debate lies in the definition of "spiritually good."

1.  **If "spiritually good" means "morally decent behavior that helps society":** Most traditions agree that unregenerate people can do this (e.g., a non-believer donating to charity).
2.  **If "spiritually good" means "an act that pleases God and is acceptable to Him":**
    *   **Reformed/Lutheran:** No. The act must be done in faith, which requires regeneration.
    *   **Arminian:** Yes, but only because God's grace enables the faith required to make the act acceptable.
    *   **Catholic:** No, not for the purpose of merit/salvation, though natural virtue is acknowledged.

### The Common Ground
Despite these differences, almost all orthodox Christian traditions agree on two points:
1.  **Salvation is by Grace:** No human work, regardless of how "good" it looks, can earn salvation apart from God's grace.
2.  **Faith is Essential:** An act is not spiritually pleasing to God unless it is rooted in faith (Hebrews 11:6). Since faith is a gift of God (Ephesians 2:8), the capacity to do true spiritual good ultimately originates from God, not the unregenerate human nature.

### Final Answer
According to the majority of historic Protestant theology (Reformed and Lutheran), **an unregenerate person cannot do anything spiritually good in God's sight** because they lack the faith required to please Him, and their motives are inherently self-centered.

However, they can perform **civil good** (actions that benefit society), which God may reward in this life, but these actions do not contribute to their standing before God or their salvation. Other traditions (Arminian, Catholic) allow for a degree of "natural good" enabled by grace, but still maintain that true spiritual merit requires regeneration.
